client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago — it was so sudden, and I don't think I've really processed it yet. The hardest part lately is feeling like everyone around me has just... moved on, like it's old news, but for me it still feels like it just happened. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep feeling this isolated.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom so suddenly, and then feeling like the world just kept moving while you're still standing in that moment of loss, that kind of loneliness can be just as painful as the grief itself. I notice there's something both urgent and exhausted in the way you're sharing this, like part of you is reaching out while another part isn't sure it's even worth trying — and I want you to know that reaching out *is* worth it, and your grief doesn't have an expiration date. We can take this at whatever pace feels right for you, and simply being here and naming what you're feeling is already a meaningful first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I appreciate you saying that, but I guess part of me is waiting for the other shoe to drop — like, where this turns into "have you tried journaling" or something that feels too simple for how big this actually is. It's not that I'm trying to be difficult, it's just that people keep offering these little fixes and it makes me feel like they don't really get how much she meant to me. She was kind of my whole support system, and now there's just this huge gap where she used to be.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, intense, like this has been building up — tells me this frustration is very real and very justified, and I want you to know I'm not here to hand you a checklist. What you're describing isn't a problem to be *fixed* with a technique; you lost the person who was your foundation, and no journal prompt touches that. So let's not pretend otherwise — I'd rather sit with you in the actual size of this loss than offer you something that makes *me* feel helpful but leaves *you* feeling unseen.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That actually... means a lot to hear, more than I expected it to. I think I've been so braced for someone to try to wrap this up neatly that I didn't realize how much I needed someone to just acknowledge that it's as big as it feels. But I'm also a little scared now, because if we're not going to fix it, then I have to just sit with the fact that she's gone and that gap isn't going to close — and I don't know if I'm ready for that.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, like something has cracked open a little — makes complete sense, because what you just touched is one of the most frightening truths of grief: that there's no fix coming, and the gap is real. But I want to gently offer this — "sitting with it" doesn't mean being alone in it, and it doesn't have to happen all at once; you don't have to be ready for the whole weight of her absence today. What you *are* doing right now, in this moment, is already braver than you're giving yourself credit for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about not being alone in it, but the honest truth is that outside of this room, I am pretty alone in it — like, my friends have stopped asking how I'm doing with it, and I don't want to keep bringing it up and feel like a burden. So the idea of "not being alone" sounds good in theory, but I'm not sure where that actually comes from in real life when the session ends.
therapist: There's something in your voice right now — soft, a little stretched thin — that tells me this isn't just a theoretical concern, this is the reality you go home to, and I don't want to gloss over that with reassurance that doesn't hold up outside this room. The fear of being a burden is worth looking at closely, because that belief — that your grief is *too much* for the people who care about you — might actually be quietly keeping you more isolated than your friends' silence alone is. That's something real we can work with together, not as a quick fix, but as a way of slowly rebuilding some of what you lost when you lost her.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I can see what you're pointing at with the "burden" thing, and honestly it stings a little because there's probably some truth to it. But I also don't think it's just a belief I've made up — my friends really have gone quiet, so it's not like I'm imagining the distance. I guess I'm just not sure how to tell the difference between protecting myself from real rejection and talking myself out of reaching out when maybe someone would actually be there.
therapist: You're holding something really nuanced here — and the careful, measured way you're working through it tells me you're thinking about this honestly rather than defensively, which takes courage. You're right that the distance from your friends is real, and it's important we don't collapse that into "just a belief" — but the question you just asked, *how do I tell the difference*, is actually the exact right question, because that's where we can do real work together. What if we started by looking at one specific person in your life and gently testing what's assumption versus what's evidence — not to prove yourself wrong, but to give you something more solid to stand on than uncertainty?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I know who I'd pick — there's one friend, Diane, who was really close with me right after it happened, but then kind of faded out over the last couple months. The thing I'm nervous about is that "testing" it sounds like I'd have to actually reach out to her, and what if she doesn't respond the way I hope — I'm not sure I have the emotional reserves right now to handle another disappointment on top of everything else. It feels like a lot to risk when I'm already running on empty.
therapist: The urgency and intensity in your voice right now makes complete sense — this isn't a small ask, and the fear of reaching out to Diane from an already depleted place is real and worth respecting, not pushing through. But I want to reflect something back to you: the way you described her — someone who *was* close, who showed up at first — suggests there's actual evidence she cares, and that's not nothing. What if reaching out didn't have to be a big vulnerable moment, but something small enough that it costs you very little — so that even an imperfect response doesn't land like a full rejection?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think I can see what you mean by keeping it small, but I'm struggling to figure out what that even looks like — like, anything I send her is going to feel loaded to me because of everything that's happened, even if it looks casual on the outside. And part of me wonders if I'm just looking for a reason to not do it, which is frustrating because I genuinely can't tell if that's self-protection or avoidance.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, like your mind is running faster than you can quite catch it — reflects exactly what you're describing, this tangle of wanting to move and not being sure you trust your own reasons for staying still. And I want to say: the fact that you can't tell if it's self-protection or avoidance isn't a failure of self-awareness, it's actually a sign that both things are probably true at once, and that's okay. What if we set aside the question of *why* for a moment and just asked — what's the smallest, lowest-stakes thing you could imagine sending Diane, something that would feel like leaving a door slightly open rather than walking through it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Maybe something like sending her an article or a meme that made me think of her — something that doesn't require her to respond with anything heavy. But even as I say that, I notice I'm already imagining her not responding at all, and that silence feeling like confirmation that I really am too much, or that the friendship has just quietly expired. I guess the door feels scary to crack open even a little when I'm not sure anything is still on the other side.
therapist: The softness in your voice as you said that — like you were bracing for something even as you were speaking — tells me this fear runs really deep, and I want to name what just happened: you came up with something genuinely good, a low-stakes, warm gesture, and then almost immediately your mind turned it into evidence of your worst fear before Diane has even had a chance to respond. That leap — from "she might not reply" to "I am too much and the friendship is over" — is worth slowing down on, because it's your grief talking, not necessarily the truth about you or about her. The door you're imagining might feel emptier than it actually is right now, and Diane deserves the chance to show you what's still there before you decide for her.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: You're right that I jumped ahead and basically wrote the whole story before anything even happened, and hearing you say that out loud makes me realize I do that a lot — not just with Diane, but with most things since my mom died. I think part of why I do it is that I got blindsided by losing her so suddenly, and now my brain is trying to protect me by predicting the worst before it can catch me off guard again. It makes sense as a survival thing, but I can also see how it's kind of sealing me off from anything that might actually help.
therapist: The way you just said that — fast, high, like something clicked into place and you needed to get it out before it slipped away — feels like a really significant moment, because what you just described is one of the most important things a person can understand about themselves: that the armor that kept you safe is now also keeping out the things you need. That insight, that your brain learned to brace for loss because loss came without warning, is not a flaw in you — it's a completely human response to an unbearable surprise. And now that you can see it, we have something real to work with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's strange because I've spent six months feeling like nothing makes sense, and now this one thing suddenly does, and I'm not sure whether to feel relieved or more scared because now I can see the pattern but I don't know how to stop it. Like, understanding why I do something doesn't automatically make it easier to do differently, and I worry that I'll leave here feeling like I had a breakthrough and then go home and just... fall right back into it. I guess I'm asking, is insight actually enough to change anything, or is this just the part where it feels meaningful in the room but doesn't hold up in real life?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, soft, pitched high like something fragile is balancing — tells me this question isn't abstract, it's urgent, and I want to answer it honestly: no, insight alone isn't enough, and you're right to name that. But here's what I'd offer — insight is the moment you realize you've been navigating in the dark, and what we do together from here is slowly build you a different way of moving through it, one small action at a time, like maybe sending that meme to Diane this week not because it will fix everything, but because it's one tiny piece of evidence you can collect against the story your brain keeps writing. The breakthrough doesn't have to hold up on its own — that's what coming back here is for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
